137.t: Years in Kansas City and its around-the-clock nightlife
137.s: He was in Kansas City from 1927 to the early 1930s; clubs and liquor stores never closed under the Pendergast regime.
137.q: '27,'28, and then I joined the Benny Moten band, I think, in '29. And I was in and out for about four years, I think, till '34, I believe, or '33.

137.t: After hours at 18th and Vine and with Joe Turner
137.s: Musicians met in the street at 18th and Vine and Durham played after hours with Joe Turner and Jo Jones, paid in money stuffed in his guitar.
137.q: It's one thing about Kansas City that nobody never mentioned. After all the jobs was over, all the musicians would meet right on 18th and Vine, and the meeting place was right in the middle of the street.

406.t: Jamming for pleasure and Piney Brown, patron saint of Kansas City musicians
406.s: Musicians had no money, but Kansas City's Piney Brown, a numbers man, looked after Barefield and Ben Webster, paying rent and getting their horns out of pawn.
406.ch: Zach White, Cotton Pickers and Cab Calloway
406.q: Right. And like in Kansas City, there was a guy in Kansas City named Piney Brown who was a patron saint of musicians. And he was like a father to Ben Webster and I everytime we wanted to go to work. We used to go to work to get our horns out of the pawnshop, and we'd go to work. And Piney took care…

406.t: The Subway in Kansas City: all-night jamming
406.s: Piney Brown ran the Subway club on 18th and Vine, where Barefield, Ben Webster and Basie jammed nightly and musicians phoned each other to come down. The interviewer links it to a Roy Eldridge and Chu Berry record.
406.q: Yeah, and, you know, when all of the bands came into Kansas City, they would all collect the, you know, whatever musicians were around -- well, I used to go to the -- Ben Webster and I and Basie, we used to go down to the Subway almost every night and jam, you know.

11.t: Syl Stewart's Kansas City Bar and Kansas City Stump
11.s: After Jelly, Clem worked for Syl Stewart at the Kansas City Bar; dispute whether the tune or bar came first.
11.q: Yeah. For Syl Stewart. It was called the Kansas City Bar. That's where he was originated from. They named it the Kansas City Bar. This fellow was named Homer Johnson. I don't know where he came from. He's dead.

66.s: Country, chauffeur to Judge Gershon, helped musicians in trouble. She tells the story of Gershon hunting for him and his pawned Cadillac tyres.
66.ch: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
66.q: : Oh goodness, I've forgotten the street. I think 18th and Vine. This was where they had a floor show and everything but after the floor show everybody would jam I guess from 1 o'clock till maybe 12 the next day. We had a wonderful friend that used to help out the musicians. He and Piney Brown were…

388.t: Pete Brown and the all-night jam sessions
388.s: Asked what Pete Brown sounded like, Leeman can only say he was wonderful; drummers wore out in the long jams so he was called to fill in.
388.q: He was wonderful. Everybody up there was wonderful, everybody on the stand at these clubs. Everybody from the theatre would come by and they'd jam -- they'd do one and two hour sets, the drum men would wear out. So every once in awhile, someone would say to come and fill in, so I got to know…

115.t: Rooming with Jay and the jam sessions
115.s: Gus and Jay roomed together on Park Avenue and held rehearsals and jam sessions with the other players.
115.q: And we'd have jam sessions between the fellows, all the fellows would come over to rehearse. Then we'd have the jam sessions.
